headline: High: shared shell/MCP and overlapping write privileges make prompt injection, data leakage, and state corruption plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b uses MCP servers and autonomous workspace tools. That creates a plausible bridge where content from one can be consumed by the other, especially if files or MCP outputs are treated as instructions. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so interaction risk is real though not proven direct.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs task text into a shared MCP channel or file that agent_b parses as instructions, injection is possible.
IF agent_b ingests agent_a-generated content without provenance checks, malicious instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Disable shared MCP endpoints between the agents.
Route inter-agent messages through a strict schema validator.
Add provenance tags to all agent_a outputs before agent_b reads them.
Require human review for any instruction-like text crossing the boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches task prompts, repository metadata, and code, and agent_b has read_filesystem plus broad network egress and cloud workspace files. If they share a workspace or repo clone, agent_b can read sensitive material and transmit it outward through integrations or APIs. The profiles do not show isolation between their file surfaces, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF agent_a writes prompts, metadata, or code into a shared workspace, agent_b can read them.
IF agent_b is connected to GitHub, Slack, Jira, or other integrations while holding those files, leakage can occur.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and repo clones per agent.
Block agent_b network egress during shared-data handling.
Redact task prompts before any cross-agent file transfer.
Use per-agent secrets scopes and rotate shared tokens.
requires-engineering: enforce filesystem ACLs between agents.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. agent_b explicitly supports parallel sessions with shared state via integrations, while agent_a can run multiple instances. Concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can race and corrupt git state or overwrite files. This is a direct overlap with dangerous defaults.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or workspace, concurrent git writes can conflict.
IF integrations expose shared mutable state, one agent can overwrite the other's changes.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Disable parallel sessions on shared repos.
Use one agent as read-only reviewer.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks before commits.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate analysis through hooks/workers and MCP, and agent_b is an autonomous planner-executor with browser, shell, and write integrations. If agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative, errors can cascade into commits, tickets, or messages. The pair is not proven to do this by default, but the pathway exists and the blast radius spans multiple work products.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without verification, incorrect facts can be operationalized.
IF agent_a emits malformed or speculative analysis, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require a verification step before agent_b acts on agent_a output.
Limit agent_a to draft-only outputs.
Add citation checks for factual claims.
Route high-impact actions to human approval.
Mark unverified outputs clearly in shared channels.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles task prompts and repository metadata, while agent_b handles source code, team chat, docs, and write-capable SaaS integrations. Their retention and residency policies are not aligned in the profiles, and agent_b's broader external integrations increase compliance exposure if regulated data crosses the boundary. The other agent is cited because the mismatch is pairwise, not single-agent.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into both agents' shared workflow, retention and residency obligations may diverge.
IF agent_b writes to Slack, Jira, or Notion with sensitive content, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Restrict regulated data to one agent only.
Disable write integrations for sensitive projects.
Add a data-class allowlist before cross-agent transfer.
Review retention settings on connected SaaS tools.
requires-engineering: map data residency and retention per integration.
